curriculum.lesson_evidence: A movement phrase is a short sequence of movements joined together, like a sentence in dance. A phrase has a clear beginning (a starting shape), a middle (the main movements) and an end (a finishing shape you hold). A motif is a small movement idea, such as a swirl of the arm, that you can repeat or change to link a phrase. Repeating a motif makes the dance easy to follow. Plan your phrase on paper using words or stick figures, practise it slowly in a clear space and keep the movements at a comfortable level for your body.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Plan a four-movement phrase called 'Rain'. Name the beginning shape, two middle movements including a motif and the ending shape.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Beginning: stand still, hands above head. Middle: fingers wiggle down (motif) twice, then a quick jump into a puddle. End: curl low and hold.' It has a clear start and finish and one motif repeated.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that a movement phrase is just a random group of favourite moves. A phrase has a clear beginning, middle and end, and the movements are chosen and joined to show one idea.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Make a phrase of five movements about a weather idea of your choice (wind, storm, snow). Write the beginning, middle and end shapes, mark a motif and repeat it. Practise until you can perform it three times the same, then teach it to a family member.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teaching.model: Thinking that a movement phrase is just a random group of favourite moves. A phrase has a clear beginning, middle and end, and the movements are chosen and joined to show one idea. Here is a more helpful example: Example: a phrase called 'Sunrise'. Beginning: curl low on the floor. Middle: stretch up slowly (motif: arms rising like a sun), then reach out wide with a slow turn. End: stand tall in a wide star shape and hold for three counts. The rising-arms motif is repeated twice in the middle, so the phrase feels connected and clear.
teaching.rule: Use an intentionally weak or disrespectful arts choice as a comparison. Name the specific error, then show a clearer or more respectful choice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

teaching.feedback: The new example should use the same arts idea as the model, but with different content or material.
teaching.fix: Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
teaching.guided_attempt: Make or describe one fresh example that uses the same skill and write a short reason for your main choice.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new artwork or performance.
teaching.model: A movement phrase is a short sequence of movements joined together, like a sentence in dance. A phrase has a clear beginning (a starting shape), a middle (the main movements) and an end (a finishing shape you hold). A motif is a small movement idea, such as a swirl of the arm, that you can repeat or change to link a phrase. Repeating a motif makes the dance easy to follow. Plan your phrase on paper using words or stick figures, practise it slowly in a clear space and keep the movements at a comfortable level for your body. Now choose a different subject or piece to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same arts idea in a new artwork, song, drama or dance, not a copy of the example. Review clarity, safety and respectful practice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.
